groups.name: conversations
groups.description: Ask, answer, dismiss, or withdraw operator decisions, with attachments and an answer form. Before writing a decision, read the writing guide: prompt-manager skill read notification-hub

commands.name: ask
commands.description: Ask the operator a decision, or revise one you already asked. The minimum is --question and either --yes-no or two --option values; everything else has a default: expires in 24h, sensitivity private, urgency normal, and an idempotency key (printed). The operator sees who is asking: the CLI names the sender from the label of your Web Console session, and --from overrides it. The operator reads it cold on a phone: write it by the guide in `prompt-manager skill read notification-hub` (a plain question, --big-picture for why it matters, --technical-details for IDs and paths), or put all three in one markdown file with --body-file. With --subject-key an ask about an ongoing situation stays one open ask: send it again with only what changes to revise it in place, with no new push. Everything you leave out stays as the open ask has it (question, options, recommendation, texts, attachments, explainer and form), and the CLI prints what it kept on stderr. A text flag replaces that text whole; give it empty ('') to clear it. A file or form question you send replaces the one with the same name or id; --remove-attachment NAME and --remove-question ID drop one, --clear-attachments and --clear-questions drop all. A keyed ask also tells the Hub you will answer the operator's "I need more context" question (--no-context-requests turns that off): answer it with --context-response, which the operator reads under their question; it is not part of the ask, so the rest of the ask stays as it is. Attach files, folders and one HTML explainer with --attach and --explainer, and add typed questions to the answer form with --form; the packet check printed to stderr says what the Hub left out or how to improve the packet. See scenarios/notification-hub/docs/concepts/DECISION_PACKETS.md. Output ends with one line `ask_id=... state=... outcome=... next: ...`; --json prints {ask_id, state, outcome, warnings[]}. outcome is created, updated (revised in place), replaced (new options: a new ask took over and pushed once), reasserted (same terms, nothing changed), suppressed (the operator dismissed these exact terms) or returned (just answered; here is that answer's ask). --and-wait waits for the answer in the same command (see --timeout) and exits with the status `wait` uses: Exit status: 0 an answer is available (answered, or the default applied); 3 the operator asked for more context, and the ask is still open; 4 your wait timed out (--timeout), and the ask is still open; 5 the ask closed without an answer (withdrawn, dismissed or expired; by id also when a revision with new options replaced it). Any other status (1) means the command itself failed: bad flags, an unreachable Hub, or a refused read. With --json the same document is printed on 0, 3, 4 and 5.

flags.name: question
flags.description: One plain sentence the operator can answer from the push alone: the choice and what it affects. No internal IDs, codes, or file paths. Required unless --body-file gives it, or --subject-key revises an open ask (which keeps its question). On a revision it replaces the question.

flags.name: option
flags.description: One option the operator can pick, as key or key=label; repeat for each (2 to 8). Or use --yes-no. The Hub adds its own free-text Other. A revision that names none keeps the open ask's options; naming them changes the options, which replaces the ask and pushes once.

flags.name: yes-no
flags.description: Shorthand for the two options yes and no. Use it when the question itself says what yes causes; otherwise write --option labels that say what each choice does. Not with --option.

flags.name: body-file
flags.description: A markdown file (or - for standard input) holding the cover text: its first paragraph is the question, ## Background the big picture, ## Details the technical details. A leading # title line is ignored. Do not also give the part it supplies as a flag.

flags.name: recommend
flags.description: The recommended option key; shown first. A revision that changes the options drops it with the old options.

flags.name: recommend-reason
flags.description: One sentence on why the recommendation is best.

flags.name: default
flags.description: Option key applied if unanswered; needs --reversible. Applies after the ask expires and at least 12 h after delivery.

flags.name: reversible
flags.description: The decision can be undone later (required for --default).

flags.name: urgency
flags.description: Default normal. high only when work is blocked right now; critical only for a real emergency, the only level that may pass quiet hours.

flags.name: context-url
flags.description: A web page that opens on the operator's phone. Never a local file path or localhost link; put those in --technical-details.

flags.name: from
flags.description: Overrides who is asking, as the operator reads it. Normally leave it out: the CLI names the sender from the label of your Web Console session, or of your run when someone named it (for example "research · steward-channel-ux-tooling"; a trailing run date such as -20261114 is dropped so one role keeps one sender across days, and the generic label "This machine" and the made-up "claude-code session <id>" labels are ignored), looked up once per command in about a second and skipped silently when it cannot be found, and the operator uses that name to tell agents apart and to filter by sender. When no label is found (a plain session nobody named, so you will show as "Agent run") the Hub names the sender itself: your service's name, or "Agent run". Pass --from only when that label would mislead: a short name of 1 to 60 characters, such as "Treasury steward". The Hub does not verify the name and never uses it for access. The session label only names an ask when it is created: a revision never renames an ask, and only a --from you give changes the name of an open one.

flags.name: big-picture
flags.description: Plain sentences for a reader with no context: what this is about, why it matters now, what each option leads to, and what happens with no answer. At most 4,000 characters. Replaces the whole text on a revision: to add to it, resend the old text and the addition (read it with `get --json`, field ask.big_picture). The answer to an operator's "I need more context" question does not belong here: use --context-response.

flags.name: technical-details
flags.description: Evidence, IDs, commands, and file paths for the agent that acts on the answer. The only place internal names belong; never what the operator needs in order to choose. At most 12,000 characters. Replaces the whole text on a revision.

flags.name: expires
flags.description: When the ask closes if nobody answers it: an RFC 3339 time, or a duration from now such as 6h. Default 24h. This is the ask's life, not how long your command waits (that is --timeout). With a duration, a resend still counts as the same request: the key is derived from the duration you wrote, not from the clock.

flags.name: sensitivity-label
flags.description: public, private, sensitive or critical: who may see the content on a device. Default private.

flags.name: idempotency-key
flags.description: Names this request so that a retry returns the same ask. Default: derived from the terms and printed (an ask without --subject-key: the same terms and expiry give the same key, changed terms a new one; a keyed ask: a fresh key per send, because the subject already makes a repeat of identical terms change nothing). Give one only to control retries yourself; reusing it with different terms is a conflict. The Hub treats a key as a retry only when it is the key of the latest request applied to that ask.

flags.name: subject-key
flags.description: Names the situation this ask is about, for example disk-pressure; always set it. Sending the same key again revises the open ask instead of adding another: identical terms change nothing, new text updates it without a new push, different options replace it, and an ask the operator dismissed is not reopened by identical terms. If the ask has already been answered or closed, a partial revision is refused with what became of the ask (read it with `get --subject-key`), and a whole ask starts a new one. 1-128 of A-Z a-z 0-9 . _ : / @ -, starting with a letter or digit.

flags.name: no-context-requests
flags.description: With --subject-key: do not tell the Hub you will answer the operator's "I need more context" question. By default a keyed ask does, and the operator is offered the button; you answer with --context-response (any revision marks the question answered, but only --context-response shows your answer to the operator). Use this when nothing will read the question (no wait, no answer), so the operator is not left waiting.

flags.name: and-wait
flags.description: After sending, wait for the answer in the same command (see --timeout) and exit with the status `wait` uses; the first `wait` needs no separate command. If it exits 3 (the operator asked for more context), answer with `ask --subject-key K --context-response '...' --and-wait`, which sends the answer and waits again. The send prints its own result first (the `ask_id=... outcome=...` line, or with --json its document), then the wait prints its result; a send that failed exits 1 before any wait starts, with its error and no `ask_id=` line. Not with --dry-run, which creates no ask to wait for.

flags.name: dry-run
flags.description: Run the packet check and show the notification the operator would get and who they would see as the sender (the name and where it came from: your --from, your session label, kept from the open ask, or named by the Hub; --json: sender and sender_source), then stop: no ask or notification is created, no file is uploaded and nothing is stored. To check the packet, the CLI does send the Hub each attachment's hash and size, and the content of the explainer page and of any Markdown file a review follows; the Hub reads them for this one check and keeps none of it. On a keyed ask the check runs on the revision merged over the open ask.

flags.name: timeout
flags.description: With --and-wait: how long your command waits for an answer, a duration such as 30m or an RFC 3339 time. Default 30m. Exit status 4 means this wait ran out; the ask stays open until it expires (--expires).

flags.name: reassert-within
flags.description: With --subject-key: close the ask if you have not sent it again for this long (a duration from 1m to 720h such as 15m). Send it on that cadence while it is still needed; a send with the same terms is outcome reasserted.

flags.name: attach
flags.description: A file or folder the operator can open inside the Hub, as PATH or PATH=LABEL (the label is only a caption); repeat for each (the Hub keeps 24, the explainer counts). The attachment's name is the file's base name, so a revision that sends a file with the same name replaces that one and the other attachments stay. A folder is one attachment: files in path order, at most 500 (extra files are left out with a warning), skipping .git, .hg, .svn, node_modules, __pycache__, .venv, .mypy_cache, .pytest_cache, .cache, .idea, .DS_Store and Thumbs.db, and never following symlinks. Each file is at most 64 MiB and all files together 256 MiB (checked from file sizes before anything is read). The Hub keeps a copy; it never serves a host path. A path that is missing, unreadable or over a limit is left out with a warning on stderr; the ask is still sent.

flags.name: explainer
flags.description: One self-contained HTML file the Hub shows sealed at the top of the decision. It is its own attachment: you do not also --attach it. It can name other attachments in src/href/poster. A revision that sends an explainer replaces the current one. Rules and a starter kit: skills/notification-hub/references/html-explainers.md.

flags.name: clear-attachments
flags.description: On a revision, drop every current attachment (the explainer included) before applying the --attach and --explainer you send. Without it a revision keeps the open ask's attachments. To drop only some, use --remove-attachment.

flags.name: remove-attachment
flags.description: On a revision, drop the current attachment with this name (its file's base name; the explainer by its name too); repeat for each. The other attachments stay. A name the ask has no attachment of is reported on stderr and changes nothing. A name you also send with --attach is replaced, not removed.

flags.name: form
flags.description: A YAML or JSON file declaring typed questions under the main options: a `questions:` list (or a bare list) of {id, type, prompt, help, required, choices, sections, sections_from, recommended, recommendation_reason, unanswered_verdict}. Types: single_choice, multi_choice, variant, section_review, text. unanswered_verdict (section_review) is what a section the operator leaves alone means: approve (default), change or drop. `recommended` is a choice key, a list of keys, a text, or a full response mapping. `sections_from: NAME_OR_PATH` makes a section_review follow the ## and ### headings of an attached Markdown file: the Hub reads the headings, and reads them again whenever a revision replaces that file, so the review always matches the document. A form file that cannot be read leaves out all questions; a broken question or recommendation is left out with a warning and the rest is kept. On a revision a question with the same id replaces the current one and the other current questions stay.

flags.name: remove-question
flags.description: On a revision, drop the current form question with this id; repeat for each. The other questions stay. An id the ask has no question of is reported on stderr and changes nothing. An id you also send in --form is replaced, not removed.

flags.name: context-response
flags.description: Your written answer to the operator's open "I need more context" question, 1-4000 characters. The operator reads it under their question on the ask, and the question is marked answered. It works on its own (`ask --subject-key K --context-response '...'` changes nothing else) or with any other change in the same command. It is kept with the question, so several rounds of question and answer stay readable. When the operator has no open question the text is not stored and a warning says so.

flags.name: clear-questions
flags.description: On a revision, drop every current form question before applying the ones in --form. Without it a revision keeps the open ask's questions and a question you send replaces the one with the same id.

commands.name: answer
commands.description: Record an answer to a pending notification question.

flags.name: note
flags.description: Optional note, stored verbatim and returned to the requester.

flags.name: responses-file
flags.description: A JSON file with the answers to the ask's form questions and notes on attachments: a list of {question_id, selected, text, sections:[{section_key, verdict, note}]}, or an object {"responses": [...], "attachment_notes": [{"attachment", "path", "note"}]} (path names a file inside a folder attachment).

commands.name: request-context
commands.description: Record the recipient's question about an open ask without answering it. The ask stays open; the requester sees the question through `conversations wait` and answers it with `ask --subject-key K --context-response '...'`.

flags.name: question
flags.description: What the recipient needs to know, 1-2,000 characters.

commands.name: dismiss
commands.description: Close an ask without recording an answer; recipient only.

flags.name: note
flags.description: Optional reason shown to the requester.

commands.name: withdraw
commands.description: Withdraw an ask you sent, by id (`withdraw <ask-id>`) or by --subject-key; it keeps its audit record. A run waiting on the ask ends with status 5 and sees your --reason. Access: by ask id you reach the asks sent from your own conversation (your run and the runs recovered from it, spawned by it or re-attached to the same harness session); by exact --subject-key you reach the ask of any run of the same owner, and that key never lists other asks. A shell with no verified identity is refused. Withdrawing follows the same rule as reading.

positionals.name: id
positionals.description: The ask to withdraw. Give the id or --subject-key.

flags.name: ask-id
flags.description: The ask to withdraw, as an alternative to the positional id. Give an id or --subject-key.

flags.name: reason
flags.description: Why the ask is no longer applicable.

flags.name: subject-key
flags.description: Withdraw the ask with this exact subject key instead of naming its id.

commands.name: wait
commands.description: Wait for an answer, for the operator to ask for more context, or for your timeout (--timeout, default 30m). Name the ask by id (`wait <ask-id>`) or by --subject-key; a restarted agent re-derives its key and waits on it. It carries on across dropped connections and the Hub's own ten-minute limit on a single wait, until the answer or your timeout. Exit status: 0 an answer is available (answered, or the default applied); 3 the operator asked for more context, and the ask is still open; 4 your wait timed out (--timeout), and the ask is still open; 5 the ask closed without an answer (withdrawn, dismissed or expired; by id also when a revision with new options replaced it). Any other status (1) means the command itself failed: bad flags, an unreachable Hub, or a refused read. With --json the same document is printed on 0, 3, 4 and 5. An answered ask prints the plain-text answer summary (the option, the note and each form answer). Output ends with `ask_id=... state=... [answer=...]`. By --subject-key the wait follows a replacement ask (new options), so it never reports a replacement as status 5; by id it does. Access: by ask id you reach the asks sent from your own conversation (your run and the runs recovered from it, spawned by it or re-attached to the same harness session); by exact --subject-key you reach the ask of any run of the same owner, and that key never lists other asks. A shell with no verified identity is refused.

positionals.name: id
positionals.description: The ask to wait on. Give the id or --subject-key.

flags.name: ask-id
flags.description: The ask to wait on, as an alternative to the positional id. Give an id or --subject-key.

flags.name: subject-key
flags.description: Wait on the ask with this exact subject key instead of its id. It follows the key: if the asker replaces the ask, the wait continues on the replacement. This is how a restarted agent resumes: re-derive the key and wait.

flags.name: timeout
flags.description: How long this command waits: an RFC 3339 time or a duration from now such as 10m. Default 30m. When it runs out the command exits 4 and the ask stays open until it expires; it does not change the ask.

flags.name: until-answer
flags.description: Keep waiting through the operator's context questions: return only on an answer, a close, or your timeout (status 0, 5 or 4, never 3).

commands.name: get
commands.description: Read one ask without changing it: options, attachments (kind, size, whether the source file still matches), form questions, the operator's responses, notes pinned to attachments, answer summary, and context requests. Name it by id (`get <ask-id>`) or by --subject-key. --json prints {ask: {...}}; a field with no value is left out, so read a missing count as 0. Access: by ask id you reach the asks sent from your own conversation (your run and the runs recovered from it, spawned by it or re-attached to the same harness session); by exact --subject-key you reach the ask of any run of the same owner, and that key never lists other asks. A shell with no verified identity is refused.

positionals.name: id
positionals.description: The ask to read. Give the id or --subject-key.

flags.name: ask-id
flags.description: The ask to read, as an alternative to the positional id. Give an id or --subject-key.

flags.name: subject-key
flags.description: Read the ask with this exact subject key instead of its id; for a run that lost its conversation.

commands.name: list
commands.description: List your asks, newest first unless you sort them. --sort attention puts what needs the operator first (escalated asks, then pending asks closing within the Hub's closing window of 6 hours, nearest first, then critical, high, normal and low urgency, then the earliest deadline, then newest); --sort due puts the earliest deadline first (an ask with none last); --sort oldest reverses newest. Narrow them with --state (--open is --state awaiting), --urgency, --sender and --query: every sort takes every filter, filters combine with AND, and the values of one filter with OR. Each row ends with the sender, an urgency other than normal, and the deadline of an ask that still waits. The summary ends with the counts by urgency and by sender under your other filters (--json: facets.urgencies and facets.senders, each a list of {value, count}); a facet's value is what --urgency and --sender take. A page holds up to --limit asks; when more follow, next_cursor (--json) or the printed hint continues from the same filters. An agent run lists only the asks of its own conversation; the owner lists all. To find an ask you sent before a restart, `list --open --query WORDS`; an ask you can name exactly is reached by its --subject-key instead.

flags.name: open
flags.description: Only asks that still wait for an answer; the shortcut for --state awaiting.

flags.name: state
flags.description: Only asks in this state: all (the default), awaiting (pending or escalated), pending, escalated, answered, defaulted, expired, withdrawn or dismissed.

flags.name: sort
flags.description: How to order the asks: newest (the default), oldest, attention (escalated first, then asks closing within 6 hours, then critical to low urgency, then the earliest deadline) or due (the earliest deadline first, asks with none last).

flags.name: urgency
flags.description: Only asks of this urgency: low, normal, high or critical. Repeat the flag or separate values with commas (--urgency high,critical).

flags.name: sender
flags.description: Only asks from this sender, named exactly as a list prints it under By sender (the whole name; a comma is part of a name, so repeat the flag for several): --sender 'Research Desk' --sender 'Agent run'.

flags.name: limit
flags.description: Page size (default 50, maximum 200).

flags.name: cursor
flags.description: Opaque continuation for the same filters.

flags.name: query
flags.description: Literal substring filter including requester identity.
